title: Centering prayer
hookLine: Thomas Keating and other monks taught a silent prayer with one sacred word

lines: DOES OUR OWN TRADITION HAVE ONE?
cards: Monks in a Massachusetts abbey kept meeting young visitors hungry for meditation, some of whom had found it on other paths.

The story told about the beginning of centering prayer is that the abbot, Thomas Keating, wondered aloud whether his own Christian tradition had a quiet practice like that, one that could be taught simply, to anyone, outside a monastery.

His fellow monks went looking. One of them, William Meninger, found an answer on a shelf, in a book this week has already opened: The Cloud of Unknowing. Out of that search came a way of praying with almost nothing in it.

teach.b: Centering prayer looks simple, and its teachers say it is. First, the door Jesus names.
Keating pointed to a line from the Sermon on the Mount: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret."
Centering prayer treats the closet as an inner room in the person.

teach.h: ONE SACRED WORD, AS A SIGN.
teach.b: Second, the sacred word. You choose one short word, like God, or peace, or love. It isn't a magic sound, and it isn't meant to be repeated constantly like a mantra or the Jesus Prayer.
In Keating's teaching, it's a sign of intention: I consent to God's presence and action within me. Third, thoughts. Thoughts will come, and that's no failure.

teach.h: THOUGHTS ARE BOATS ON A RIVER.
teach.b: Keating compared them to boats going by on a river. You don't chase them and you don't fight them. When you notice you've climbed aboard one, you return, ever so gently, to the sacred word.
Then you let even the word fade.
Fourth, consent, the heart of it. Centering prayer doesn't try to produce a feeling, a vision, or a calm mind. It's an act of saying yes, again and again, without words.
Keating taught that the fruit shows up later, in ordinary life, not during the prayer itself. Some practice it with a group, and Keating suggested a longer sit than today's, twice a day.
The shape is the same at any length: a word, a yes, and a lot of gentle returning.

how: People who practice centering prayer sit in silence with eyes closed, gently returning to a chosen sacred word when they notice thoughts, sometimes in groups that meet in churches and retreat houses.

o: a group prayer led from the center of a circle
a silent prayer resting on one word, as a sign of consent
a prayer for balancing the body's energy centers

p: a sign of intention and consent
boats going by on a river

s: in centering prayer, the sacred word is repeated constantly, like a mantra
in Keating's teaching the word is a sign of consent, returned to gently only when you notice you've drifted.
having thoughts during centering prayer means it failed
thoughts will come. you notice, and return gently to the word.
the monks who shaped it drew on The Cloud of Unknowing
the old English book with its one short word was one of their sources.

games.q: you're sitting in centering prayer and realize you've spent a while planning dinner. what do you do?
o: stop and start the prayer over from the beginning.
return, ever so gently, to the sacred word.
push the thought away hard so it won't come back.
games.why: no scolding and no fighting. you return gently to the sacred word, and let it fade again. the returning is the prayer.

practice: Choose a short word now: if you pray, a word like God or peace; if not, a word like yes, or open. Let it settle once, quietly, then sit.
When you notice you've drifted off on a thought, a plan, a memory, even a good insight, come back gently to the word without scolding yourself, and let it go again; the returning is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Centering prayer. A silent Christian prayer with one sacred word, used as a sign of consent, and returned to gently whenever thoughts carry you off. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 6:6: the closet: an inner room or storeroom.

carryVoice: Your line: consent. A quiet yes, said again and again, without any words. Until tomorrow.
